items.title: A Game Boy Color playing an old black-and-white game in colour
items.detail: Today cBoy runs a black-and-white-only cartridge as a plain Game Boy, and asking it to be a Color for one gives a white screen. A real Game Boy Color colours those games: its start-up code picks a colour scheme from a table keyed by the title's checksum (with the title's fourth letter to tell apart games that share a checksum), or the scheme the player chose by holding a button combination while it starts (Up, Up+A, Up+B, Left, Left+A, Left+B, Down, Down+A, Down+B, Right, Right+A, Right+B), writes those colours into the colour palette memory, switches itself into compatibility mode, and the game's own three black-and-white palette registers then pick from those colours. cBoy ships no start-up code, so reproduce that result in Rust: the table is documented in Pan Docs ('Power Up Sequence', compatibility palettes) and SameBoy's own open-source start-up code has the same table; take the data from the documentation, not by copying code. When the player HAS installed a real Color start-up file, the real one must run and give the same result. Settings: keep today's behaviour as the default for everyone (a black-and-white game still looks like a Game Boy unless the player chooses otherwise), and add one plain choice for black-and-white games, for example 'Colour for black-and-white games': 'Off (like a Game Boy)' / 'Automatic (like a Game Boy Color)' / the twelve schemes in plain names. Fit it to the existing options (.kiro/notes/docs/CBOY_OPTIONS_INVENTORY.md and options.rs) and regenerate the inventory. Works on both drawers. Tests: the scheme chosen for a header (including a shared checksum split by the fourth letter, and an unknown game getting the default scheme), each manual scheme, the registers a Color leaves in compatibility mode, a black-and-white test picture coming out in the expected colours, and nothing changing for colour games or for anyone who leaves the setting alone.

items.title: Where an IO write lands inside its M-cycle (the last black-and-white Mealybug picture)
items.detail: .kiro/notes/docs/CBOY_EXACT_DRAWER.md says the last DMG picture's four wrong pixels come from the dot on which a CPU write to an IO register reaches the picture hardware, which lives in bus.rs (yours tonight). Implement the hardware's timing for that, following SameBoy's model of when each register write takes effect relative to the dot, with a one-line comment per rule naming the behaviour. Mealybug must go up or stay the same, never down, and the Standard drawer must not change.
